title: How to Resolve Pop-Up Debate Power Struggles Where a Student Refuses to Speak -to-speak
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart addresses what to do when a student flatly refuses to participate in a pop-up debate rather than having an official speaking accommodation. His method: quickly and calmly move on during the debate itself to avoid a public power struggle, then privately pull the student aside afterward to ask what happened, offer help, and invite them to try again next time, with no shame attached. He frames pop-up debates as low-stakes precisely so a missed debate isn't a high-pressure event. He argues this approach works because it minimizes shame, which compounds anxiety, models for the rest of the class that setbacks are normal and don't need to derail the room, and, over years of use, eventually gets even reluctant students participating. The piece closes with his broader philosophy that increasing pressure on a reluctant speaker is counterproductive; patience and quiet follow-up work better than public insistence.
points: Handling a refusal-to-speak moment during the debate itself, not after, matters: moving on quickly and without comment prevents a public power struggle and limits shame in front of peers.
The follow-up conversation is where the real work happens — Stuart asks what happened, offers help, and reframes the missed credit as a low-stakes grade rather than a punitive one.
Reducing shame is the operating principle: mixing shame with a student's existing speech anxiety creates what Stuart calls a toxic and living cocktail that feeds upon itself.

Increasing pressure on a non-speaking student is the wrong move — normalizing setbacks for the rest of the class and giving the student a second chance next week is what eventually gets reluctant speakers participating.
quotes: When there is a lull in a pop-up debate, I am quick to call on students who have not yet spoken. I do this to save instructional time, to limit unhelpful awkwardness, and to reduce unhelpful pressure.
I make a note on my clipboard to remind me to touch base with the student — usually just an underline or a 0. I then move on to calling the next person who hasn't spoken yet.
Well, for today's debate, you didn't get any credit, but that's okay — we'll be having another one next week. My question to you is, what can I do to help you make that debate a success?
Well first of all, I think it's the best way because it reduces shame. Most of us experience some degree of anxiety in speaking for our peers. For some of us, this anxiety is debilitating.

I know that, whenever you mix shame in with anxiety, it's a toxic and living cocktail that feeds upon itself. So, by moving on quickly from the refusal to speak, I'm giving shame as little sunlight as possible.

The last thing you want to do for someone who is refusing to speak publicly is place more pressure to speak upon them. And when we turn situations like these into anything other than what I've described above, that's what we do: we increase pressure and shame.
